utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case please, Mr. Court Deputy.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is Case Number IT-01-48-T, the Prosecutor versus Sefer Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Did you have a good rest yesterday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, Mr. Weiner, do you have any re-direct examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes, just brief, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: SIMUN ANDJELINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yesterday on page 69 you were asked about the possibility of the victims being killed by explosive devices or hand grenades and you answered no. The first thing I would like to ask you about is you were asked about artillery and your answer isn't clear. Were any of these individuals killed as a result of artillery devices or bombs or whatever?

utterances.speaker: SIMUN ANDJELINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we're talking about artillery weapons, what I mean by that is that that artillery weapon, once it hits the place that is the target, it explodes. And in that sense, we differentiate between explosive wounds and not artillery wounds in forensic medicine. On the other hand, there are artillery guns of smaller calibre which are used for anti-aircraft defence. It's that type of artillery. Therefore, your question is not specific enough, it's not precise. As far as the projectiles which cause an explosion once they hit the ground, such explosive wounds were not found on these 27 bodies. And I also did not find that there was any activity by larger projectiles because these type of wounds look completely different on the body.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, that was my next question. Had you ever performed autopsies prior to September 1993 where victims had suffered wounds from -- explosive-type wounds or wounds from artillery?

utterances.speaker: SIMUN ANDJELINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, those were very common causes of death because people would enter a minefield or they would die from shelling. So in my work I did have such cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And just could you tell us, what's the level of difficulty in distinguishing between explosive-device wounds and those caused by bullets?

utterances.speaker: SIMUN ANDJELINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, in order to answer this I would like to refer to my drawing, if I may be allowed to do so. If I could have that on my computer screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That's P413.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, you have the pen in your hand. Are you planning to draw?

utterances.speaker: SIMUN ANDJELINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] No, just to show. No, just to show what I already tell. [Interpretation] As I have shown here in the left-bottom corner, right here, when there is fragmentation and when these fragments enter the body, on the borders of the wound we can see dirt, as a result of the fact that the fragments of the explosive device are smeared with gunpowder particles. Also, the wound is of an irregular shape and in the depths of the wound we can see numerous contusions. There is another characteristic of an explosive wound. It is very difficult to find one wound. On the body of a person we will always find more than one wound which are due to the action of the fragments of such an explosive device. And given the nature of the explosion, these wounds are found in a close group and it is very easy to determine the direction from which the explosion came, i.e., the place where the explosive device was. In other words, explosive wounds are very typical in more than one way and it is very easy for forensic pathologist to recognise them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, sir. Now, yesterday on page 45 you were asked about contusions to the left ear and you answered: "The contusions can be seen much better on the original photographs." Do you have those original photographs with you and can you show them to us?

utterances.speaker: SIMUN ANDJELINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please give me the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir. Number 23.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: SIMUN ANDJELINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have them. When I used this technology, there is reflection of light, so the picture is not really very clear. Maybe this photo should be scanned or maybe the original should be shown. I don't know. This technology does not lend its to very good interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, sir, if we all approached you with the picture, is it better visible on that photograph?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, could we approach the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Or could the witness approach the Judges and then the counsel? However you want to do it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, you may show that picture to the Defence and then put it to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: There's no objections at all to the Court having a look. I should raise this, Your Honours. It does raise an issue that ought to be addressed, and that is if the Prosecution proposes to rely on a particular photograph, that's the one we should really on. Frankly, that is a much clearer photo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we'll have to have it scanned in. But could we approach the witness and have him demonstrate?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But apparently it's not working on the -- could Your Honours approach and all counsel approach. Because at this point we can't do it by ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I believe I've seen that picture already and you just do whatever it is. We know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. If they twist it it's working.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Could you please show us the cutting line or whatever you were referring to yesterday -- you said it was better -- you could better see the contusion.

utterances.speaker: SIMUN ANDJELINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I showed this yesterday on the copy. This is the cutting edge which is lost in the hair and is not very well visible. And then we see it posteriorly. This part is not so well visible because it is a lateral and a posterior, and this part here is part of the earlobe that is preserved. At the bottom of this cut and on the borders, you can see tissue which is contused.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you have any other photographs that would also assist on this?

utterances.speaker: SIMUN ANDJELINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but it is almost an identical photo which would not tell us anything new.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we'll try and scan them or have them copied as best we can.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Do you have the original negatives to those photos?

utterances.speaker: SIMUN ANDJELINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And finally --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: May I just raise one matter. Sorry, I don't mean to interrupt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Could the Defence please be provided with a hard copy of the scanned photograph when that's done for our future purposes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, sir, finally on pages 63 to ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No problem, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Finally on pages 63 to 65 you were asked about having not performed certain tests such as swabbing and analysis of gunpowder, recovery and analysis of the bullets, internal analysis of the path of the bullets. Would these analyses have changed your opinion as to the cause of death of those individuals?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, I would object to that question. The issue is -- it's not a question of whether the analyses would have changed the opinion. It depends on what the analyses says, one might infer. But in any event it's a question that seems to be entirely speculative, so I object to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I believe this question is the natural course following up with the previous one you asked in the proceedings. So in this sense, this question is allowed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've already said in my testimony that the wounds on the body are of such a nature and characteristics that an additional analysis and especially pathological, histological analysis would not shed any new light, nothing that is not already known in medical literature. Obviously the analysis of gunpowder particles would be useful if this was compared with the weapon that may have been involved in the crime. This would serve to positively establish which weapon was used to fire. As far as my part is concerned, the part that was relative to the cause of death, the analysis in question would not provide me with anything new -- any new information that would have served to change my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Witness, I appreciate your testimony very much since I am a layman in this field. So I benefitted a lot from your testimony, especially that drawing. I just have a general question for you. Judging from the wounds on the deceased, can you establish whether the wound was inflicted purposely or incidentally?

utterances.speaker: SIMUN ANDJELINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. This cannot be told from the wounds. This is why in forensic pathology when dealing with the cases of murder almost always during the trial have the so-called combined expertise where we analyse the facts that the ballistic experts have to deal with. They record all the physical evidence found on the spot such as different traces on the walls, the place from which the bullets were fired and where casings were found. After that, what we do is reconstruction of the crime. During the reconstruction the initial part of an on-site investigation involves the measurement of the distance between the body and the evidence. And this part is very important to establish the direction and the distance from which the projectile had been fired as well as the position and relationship, physical relationship, between the victim and the perpetrator. And finally, we do the so-called combined forensic expertise which involves ballistic experts and forensic pathologists. And during that stage, a -- certain assertions by the perpetrator are either confirmed or rejected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. And just one more question. Can you establish the time or time frame when the wounds were inflicted by examining the wounds on the bodies of the deceased?

utterances.speaker: SIMUN ANDJELINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What we can establish with precision is whether a wound was inflicted during the life of the deceased or post-mortem. This can be concluded based on the appearance of the wound and the so-called vital reactions along the borders of the wound. After the death, after the blood flow no longer exists, such traces disappear completely and the wound looks completely different. This is something that can be established for a fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: But you could not say for sure that the wound was inflicted 24 hours ago or a week ago?

utterances.speaker: SIMUN ANDJELINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This can be done indirectly by looking at the body and the stage of its deterioration. Because it is well-known that death spots appear some three or four hours after death, rigour mortis sets in some one or two hours after death. These are the signs that appear on the body which we use not for the precise determination of the time of death but just for an orientation. Also, we can measure the internal temperature of the body and also in forensic pathology we use maggot larvae because it is well-known how long their biological cycle of multiplication is. All these are methods which help us to establish indirectly how much time passed between the time of death and the examination of the dead body.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any questions out of my questions? I see none. At this stage, are there any documents to tender?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes. The autopsy reports. The autopsy reports start at page 1 and run approximately 154 pages. The first eight pages of the autopsy report are various letters. I looked at it last night - from different people. Those aren't necessary. Page 9 that has the lists of those persons who were examined and the dates of birth, that's really the first page of -- that should be considered because it lists the victims in order. So we would ask that MFI 409 be admitted from page 9 to 154 and we not consider the various letters from different people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, that seems to be a pragmatic approach. We don't require them to be removed. They just have nothing much to do with the evidence. And otherwise there is no objection to relevant material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. That report is admitted into the evidence. I guess there's no documents from the Defence side?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Witness -- yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: There is actually one more matter. The witness was given by Defence a photograph last evening -- oh, at the end of the day to see whether he recognises the photograph and I don't know what the answer is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, you'll recall -- there was a photograph that was in the book of photos provided by the Defence and when I started to question the witness about it he wasn't sure that he had ever seen it before. Perhaps it would be appropriate if I could ask the witness one question about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Doctor, pardon me to renew the cross-examination now. You recall a photograph was given to you yesterday. Do you have any recollection of seeing it or any comment you can make about that particular photograph?

utterances.speaker: SIMUN ANDJELINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I made an effort yesterday when I came back from the Tribunal and I found this photo among the originals. And I apologise to Mr. Morrissey for this and I would like to point out that this is one of the photos that are identical to the original and they concern Mrs. Anica Stojanovic, number 26.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I'm very grateful for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, since that's been identified, I had a question that I wanted to ask about it. The Prosecutor should of course be entitled to re-examine on it if need be, but what I be permitted to do that in light of the answers?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Doctor, sorry to bite the apple a second time here. But could I just ask you this. Now that you have that photograph, I'm grateful to you for finding it, what does that indicate? Is it an entry wound? Can you indicate whereabouts?

utterances.speaker: SIMUN ANDJELINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: An entry wound.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Can you indicate -- although you didn't perform an internal examination of Anica Stojanovic, can you indicate what -- given what you know about the entry and the exit wound, what vital organs inside the body were endangered by that wound?

utterances.speaker: SIMUN ANDJELINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I can see, one can say that the endangered organs are the liver, the lower part of the lungs, in other words some vital organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Now, I understand that you didn't perform an internal examination, but it's at least possible that that injury itself was a fatal injury, likely to lead to death without any others. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMUN ANDJELINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: All right. And just finally, it's evident to you that that injury by virtual of its characteristics was an injury inflicted during life or at least when the body was capable of responding to the injury. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMUN ANDJELINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Those are the questions I had. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any questions out of this picture?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No. I'd like just the ERN number for that photo. I think it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Sorry, Your Honour. The ERN number is 0361-7475. Now, I just want to be sure that it's in the book that Your Honours have that was tendered, otherwise I'll tender it separately. It's in my book but -- so that's the number 0361-7475.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Mr. Morrissey, we have that in the collection of photos.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I'm grateful for that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you have any questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes, just one brief one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, you indicated that there was a gunshot wound to the head and there's one to the body, which is the one that you just saw. From looking at those wounds, can you determine which one came first?

utterances.speaker: SIMUN ANDJELINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've already said to the Presiding Judge, it is very difficult to establish that just by looking at the wounds. What I can say for a fact is that both entry wounds and both exit wounds were inflicted during the life of the person because there is a vital reaction on the body. If you want me to give you another opinion, I believe that during the incident the first wound to inflict -- to have been inflicted was the one in the chest. Although the vital organs were endangered, the victim may have survived and remained living for a while. After the head injury, the head injury caused an instant death because most of the head had been shattered and the brain had been destroyed. And that is why I believe that in the course of events the first wound that was inflicted was the wound in the chest and in the back. And then the next wound was the one on the head.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness, for coming to The Hague to give your evidence. We appreciate you coming very much. Madam Usher will show you out of the courtroom and we wish you a very pleasant journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: As I promised you yesterday, we'll give some time to Defence to present his harsh argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's amazing how a night's rest can get rid of harshness and leave us with an argument, which I will attempt to present in a sensible way rather than harshly. Your Honours, what we propose to do this afternoon is to file a -- some written arguments. Formally we'll do it by way of a motion because that gives everyone the opportunity to deal with it. Probably in a reality it's a response to Prosecution's intention expressed by my learned friend to tender a part of a report. So we'll do that in writing, but I have to really place on record some of the concerns that we have so that the Prosecutors know if it's not entirely clear in our written submissions what our concerns are so that the Tribunal knows what is at issue. By way of introduction, these are just introductory remarks, I would say this. The witness Mr. Ridgway has been engaged in this matter for over two years and his report was provided to the Defence long ago. At the time it was provided, it relied upon a great deal of material that was provided by the Prosecutor. That expert material was given to the Prosecutor along with a brief and some requests as to what he should give his opinion about. Now, Your Honours, everything's changed in respect of that. The Prosecutors decided not to call a great deal of that material. Furthermore, so that the statements upon which his evidence rests have been -- many of them have been withdrawn, more than half in fact have been withdrawn. Likewise, a great deal of the exhibits -- or the of the, if you like, orders, documents, articles, and so on which were provided to him have not found their way into evidence and have nothing to do with this case. On that basis he provided an opinion on the -- on that material. So what you have is an opinion from Mr. Ridgway that's based on a certain set of facts, certain matrix of factual material. Now the Prosecutors by the letter that we've been provided with and by some answers by Mr. Re in court yesterday have indicated that this witness will still give the same opinion even if the factual matrix changes. And they assert that even though they haven't talked to him about it. Now, you would be very concerned if any such witness, whether an expert or not an expert, exists in the world, in other words that their opinion is going to remain the same regardless of the changes in the evidence or the evidential basis for those opinions. Now, when it's asserted by the Prosecutors here that Mr. Ridgway is going to say the same thing, we're very concerned by that because we think most witnesses -- well, not witnesses generally but expert witnesses who are here to give opinion evidence give the opinion after they've considered the evidence. But in this case we have a different situation being asserted by the Prosecutors that he's going to give that opinion even though he hasn't seen the new material or is not aware of the new material and hasn't received any of the new material such as has arisen in the course of the trial. So we are very concerned about what nature of expert we are dealing with here. Is it a person who brings an opinion first and then gets the evidence to justify that opinion, or is it a real expert who looks at the evidence and then forms an opinion? And it's the reason why I asked for clarification yesterday from Mr. Re as to whether Major General Ridgway has an idea of what's coming his way and whether he agrees with the things that have been said in court here. Because quite frankly, they want to call him on the 25th. That's 12 days away, and at the moment they're not telling this Court -- the Prosecutors are not telling you that he has agreed to give any such evidence at all. What the Prosecution in that letter have told you what they expect and hope he will say. But -- there's number of criticisms that can be made about that position but the most fundamental one is that that's just not going to assist the Tribunal in any way. Because in the future you're going to be presented, if the Prosecution account is accurate, with an opinion of a witness who's just going to readjust the evidential basis for a pre-existing opinion. Now, that cannot be right. That cannot be allowed. And that's an initial introductory criticism here and it's one which we take very seriously because what it's really presuming that the opinions are given and that the evidence for the opinion doesn't matter. Now, we're very concerned about it. We don't think that the Prosecution are bringing a proper approach to bear on the calling of this witness. Now, we've got some substantive issues that we have to raise about that of course as well -- actually, before I come to the substantive ones there's one more procedural one. We want to make it quite clear that it is an unacceptable position to advance for the Prosecutors that this man be called for one day on the matters that he's going to testify about. I could indicate that prior to the Prosecutor adding the new things they want to lead from this witness, I would have taken four days with this witness. Now, I would have done that because he deals with expert material and that he would therefore have to be confronted with document after document. If he hasn't been shown the full range of documents, he would be confronted with those. In addition, where he's relied upon statements by witnesses who did in fact give evidence here, he would have to be confronted with their specific answers, and I have in mind particularly the evidence of Mr. Karevelic but also the evidence of Jusuf Jasarevic; Nermin Eminovic, and the SVB witnesses; Selmo Cikotic, the commander of Operations Group Zapad; and a number of other military -- of the more senior people who had testified in this case. And I would be sued for incompetence if I didn't properly confront him with that material because we think -- obviously the Defence has got a lot of things to say about him. But at the very least, that's what I would have to do. The suggestion that we can deal with him in one day is not sustainable. The suggestion that we could deal with him in two days is simply not sustainable either. I have to deal with this man properly. Some witnesses you can tell a -- you can crush down the evidence a little bit. We did it with Mr. Karevelic because we didn't want to have a gap there. So the Defence got a day effectively -- effectively a limited period of time to cross-examine Mr. Karevelic. But it's different with an expert. You've got to put the case to him properly. It's not a question of us being wordy or lengthy, we just need that period of time. I'm not aware of any other case at this Tribunal where a military expert has been called on this basis that the Prosecutor wants to call, whereby they give you half of a report with most of the evidence taken out that they don't like; Some extra material is led from the witness which we've got no notice at all; and then the Defence is given a couple of hours to cross-examine so an important person can go about his important business, leaving the accused in the position that he is now. It is in my submission not to be taken seriously that the Prosecution should have a day, even if it's an extended session, to cross-examine this person. And we're very concerned about it. We think the Prosecutor knows that that might be accepted by the Court -- I'm not presuming what ruling Your Honour might make about it, but what I'm putting is that we're very concerned that the Prosecutors are setting up a situation where they'll argue they can bring an expert in rebuttal rather than bring it in their case now. And we're very worried about that. In other words, that they would now say to the Court, well, we can't call Mr. Ridgway. We're not able to call him because he can only come for one day and that's not acceptable, so we just won't call him and then seek later on to say, oh, but now we can. So we're very worried by that. Obviously it's a matter of concern to the Defence because all through this case there's been the question of this expert, all along there's been a hanging question: What's he going to say? Is he going to be called at all? And now we've come to this incredible position at the end of the Prosecution case which you couldn't have predicted in the past, that we would find ourselves here, now, where the Prosecution are telling us that they still want to call him; they haven't spoken with him; they don't know if he agrees with the report that they propose to tender, which is a report effectively edited by Mr. Re and not by the witness. So in short, that timing issue is one that is of real concern and one at the moment is an unacceptable argument. Now, the next thing I want to put is that the Prosecution have got to comply with some basic fundamental requirements when they lead expert evidence. They've got to give you a report. The reason for that is so that the Chamber and the Defence can respond to that report, prepare cross-examination, brief experts, deal with experts, assemble the material to be put to the witness. All of those things. But now we're confronted with this amazing situation, frankly, that we're going to be dealing with Ramiz Delalic next week, potentially Mr. Alispahic, if he's coming, after that. And then we'll come to the expert. And really, we're going to be busy. I personally am going to be very busy at that time. Naturally, we have prepared some cross-examination for Mr. Ridgway. We did that a long time ago. We still don't know what he's going to say. When I come to the substance of the Prosecutor's letter, well I'll indicate to the Court the new things that are coming and we still don't know what they are; we just know there are categories of things. So that's the first thing. We need a report. We need something to work with. We need it to have spelled out and it has to have footnotes and it has got to be sourced. Your Honours, it's fundamental when experts are called that they give evidence about something that's a proper field of expertise and that's got to be spelled out. And it's not proper to call someone to give evidence about international humanitarian law. The expert in that field is Your Honour and your colleagues on the Bench. And it's precisely that issue that you are the best place to judge and have to judge. Of course, military experts can give helpful evidence outside the normal experience of the Tribunal and which can assist you in particular fields, for example relating to military structures and so on; perhaps in relation to local practice they can give that evidence. A British military expert might be able to give some evidence about British military practice and that might be of some assistance to the Court. But that issue has got to be dealt with. And at the moment we've got a substantive objection which will be in the motion. But when dealing with expert evidence, Your Honours, it's crucially important that that be testable. It's got to be testable. The factual basis of the opinion has to be available for scrutiny. Without a report, it's not. The current report, even if it was cut in the way that is proposed by the Prosecutor, would still be based upon a factual matrix of statements by witnesses and materials which may or may not be in evidence in the form in which was viewed by General Ridgway at the time he compiled his report two years ago. Now, we very much doubt that he'll have time to look at this material properly. We think that what is likely he'll come along here ill-prepared and unable to deal with the sort of questions because he won't have time to prepare it. If he's not able to have time to spend in court answering questions, it's hard to imagine that he will have time to read the transcripts of evidence that were here and look properly at the material provided to him. Nor has the Prosecutor said anything to indicate to the contrary and it seems incredible that it would be so. Now, all of that adds up to one thing: They should have given us a report long ago. They haven't. Today we don't have a report. And according to this letter, next week we're still not going to have a report. And in fact it's the Prosecution's plan that we never will have. Now, look next of all at the new material the Prosecutor wants to lead. Your Honours, the Prosecutors have indicated that they want to lead additional oral evidence from him on the specific measures that a commander should take to prevent breaches of international humanitarian law. Now, that's problematic. It's doubtful that that evidence can be given in this court. It's up to you to decide that question, not him. You may be assisted by British practice, what steps they take, but if the Prosecutor wants to lead that -- and of course the British, it might be said, very often get things right but not always, not always. No always. But in any event that could be of some assistance to the Court. So if the Prosecutor had given proper notice about that long ago, it may be that we would have prepared and said, okay, we'll deal with that. But we're still not being told that's the case and it's only my surmise that that's one of the things that they might seek to lead through this witness. They haven't said so. They haven't told us what they're going to lead; it's 12 days away. They've also indicated -- as you will see, "We will anticipate leading brief oral evidence from the general in relation to several aspects of his report." Now, they haven't said what aspects nor what additional material he's going to provide. Now, this is not a situation of proofing notes. We don't like proofing notes on the Defence side. It's been made clear throughout the trial. Whatever our position may be about proofing notes, proofing notes are not an substitution for an expert report. This is not a witness who is coming along and might say when he gets here, I've suddenly remembered seeing the gun, or remembered seeing a red car. That's different, that's -- we're all grown-ups here in court and we can deal with those sorts of things. Not when it's an expert. Not when it's material that needs preparation and needs briefing. Now, those are the only things I want to raise in advance here. We're going to put this in a motion because we've got substantive objections to this witness's evidence in any event. I'm not going to go through it now; it's in the motion, but they relate to issues of invading the Tribunal's territory, giving evidence about the ultimate issue of guilt of innocence of Mr. Halilovic and other things about the factual conclusions on which his evidence is based. We can put all that in the motion and we will. At the moment I regret to say we're being put in a position by the Prosecution of impossibility. We think it would be -- well, we think it's a very unfair manoeuvre, frankly, to leave it to this late to announce the course, as they have, then to announce this course which itself which is an spectacularly unfair one, in our submission. And finally, not to be accountable by way of providing a report which can be dealt with in the normal, sensible way. Now, the practice in other Chambers is always adapted to the facts of those cases. We're not seeking to say that you're bound by any other practice. But to come with expert evidence -- in fact, effectively the only expert evidence relating to military structures and so on to be called by the Prosecutors in this frankly ill-prepared and half-baked way, we say it's -- reflects a state of uncertainty about their own case. But whatever it may reflect about their certainties or uncertainties, it exposes the Defence to grave unfairness and we regret that it's happened. We oppose it happening. Our submission is going to be that this witness shouldn't be called at all. He simply shouldn't be permitted to give evidence at this stage. He's not going to help you. That argument will be in the motion. It's not just a question of him not helping. It's a question of the Defence being exposed now to a position of -- well, it wouldn't happen in the common-law system. It would never happen in the civil system. This Tribunal here sets the highest standards, not the lowest ones, and this ad hoc expertise is just not to be permitted. And that's the matter I wish to raise this morning. I've got some other matters not concerned with the expertise, but perhaps we can deal with those later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I believe we should give the opportunity for the Prosecution to respond to this very issue first and later on we'll deal with other matters. Any response?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Several points I would just briefly address. My learned colleague has said he will file a motion. The Prosecution will of course respond when we receive the motion. Our initial position is that we're entitled to call an expert, a military expert, to give limited evidence in a particularly specialised field. If the Defence wish to challenge the qualifications of a lieutenant general in the British army who has served in high positions in Kosovo and the Balkans and his ability to give expert opinion as to the measures a commander should take to, A, prevent, or B, punish perpetrators, assuming notice of offences which have been committed, they are entitled to challenge his qualifications. The Prosecution's answer to the challenge of qualifications is that this general is as well qualified as any other who has given expert evidence before this Tribunal. The Tribunal -- of course the Trial Chamber is aware that General Karevelic spent something like I think -- spent several weeks in the Hadzihasanovic case giving his expert testimony. And the Prosecution didn't challenge Mr. Karevelic's expertise to give evidence on a slightly different matter. The Prosecution's view is that the -- this person is -- this person, his level of seniority and expertise in the field is as well qualified as anyone to give evidence on those two matters. Mr. Morrissey has also referred to the time. Well, that's a matter which we can deal with at the time if the Defence require more time for cross-examination. A lot depends upon the answers they're getting and where they're going with a witness. Some witnesses often you feel you need a lot of time with and events turn out, if you're particularly focussed, that you don't. And the Prosecution's view of looking at the anticipated scope of General Ridgway's evidence that if it's dealt with effectively in cross-examination, there's material there for the Defence if they want it because the general is making a lot of assumptions and his report does give -- does give some stuff for the Defence there. So it depends on how they deal with it. It's ultimately a matter of submission, in our respectful submission -- I mean submission at the end of the day, at the end of the case. It's not quite true that experts are not limited in other cases. Mr. Weiner and I myself had experience of two particular experts in the Simic, Tadic, and Zaric case in which the Defence called two experts in one day and the Trial Chamber gave us I think an hour each to cross-examine these witnesses. So there is a direct precedent for experts to be limited to a certain matter and the cross-examination to be limited. I'm certainly not suggesting that be done here, but it is certainly not something that is unheard of before this Tribunal for cross-examination to be limited according to how it will help the Trial Chamber. Complaint is also made about the difference between proofing notes and -- or notes or letters and a report. The Prosecution's position on this is we are -- the Tribunal should not be particularly interested in the Defence's repeated complaint about the fact that Mr. Morrissey doesn't like proofing notes. There's a very well-reasoned decision in the Limaj case recently which goes through the Tribunal jurisprudence and practice in the common law and civil law and quite clearly comes down in the favour of the practice of providing proofing notes to the Defence; and vice versa, the Defence providing proofing notes to the Prosecution in anticipation of a witness's testimony. And the decision goes into great detail about the differences between an international Tribunal, where witnesses are not that easy to come by and some years take -- years pass between when a witness is first interviewed and often before an indictment is confirmed, when they ultimately testify and a domestic situation where the witnesses are basically, in most cases, located in a very short distance from the Prosecutor and the court -- the cases are heard relatively quickly, relative to the event that is being litigated. The object of proofing notes is to provide -- or letters or pre-trial briefs is to provide notice to the other side of the effect of the evidence, to give them the chance to respond to it. It doesn't matter, in our submission, whether it's in the form of a report, a letter, a filing, or a proofing note. The effect is the same: It's notice to the other side. If they have notice of what the person is going to say, they have time to prepare. Now, as to the substance of the general's anticipated evidence, there are two areas in which the Prosecution seeks -- primarily seeks the benefit of the general's expertise, and that is his expert opinion as to the measures which a commander should take to prevent breaches of international humanitarian law, and similarly, to punish breaches of international humanitarian law. It's not correct, as the Defence -- learned Defence counsel says, to say that the expertise in this area rests solely within the breasts of the Judges. It quite clearly doesn't. The Defence must have done their own research, especially into the law on failure to prevent breaches of international humanitarian law. And the law of this -- jurisprudence of this particular Tribunal is spectacularly thin on the ground in relation to the specific measures a commander should take, assuming the commander has notice, inquiry notice, that a breach may occur. And that's where the Tribunal must obtain the benefit of expert assistance as to what -- as to the interaction between military law and practice. That is what a commander can do. And things that a military manual won't tell you, such as in a situation with a failure to punish, assuming there's a combat situation. What should a commander do in, for example, Grabovica? Is combat going on? Is the commander obliged to stop the combat and to isolate the perpetrators, to take them away, have them investigated on the spot, or may the commander to allow those troops suspected of committing crimes go into combat? The military manuals, the laws, the regulations won't tell you. It's only something an expert can say or someone with very senior rank can say, well, in this situation, I would weigh up the following and based upon law, based upon doctrine, this is what a commander should do or could do in those circumstances. You won't find that in the jurisprudence of this Tribunal, you won't find that in the military regulations, you'll find that only from expert evidence. Now, we do have some expert evidence before the Tribunal. General Karevelic gave some evidence as to the failure to -- as to the measures a commander should take to punish. And the Prosecution is generally satisfied with that and it generally covers that area. The area which we don't have the evidence on at the moment is the failure to prevent and that's where we want General Ridgway to provide an opinion. In the Prosecution's submission, that is not a difficult matter for the Defence to deal with because they must have their own expert, Brigadier Dzambasovic or whoever, has their own opinion which may be the same or may be different as to that. And they're quite entitled to put their own expertise or their own suggestions to General Ridgway, assuming he says what we anticipate he'll say and deal with him in that manner. The Defence also suggested that it was some sort of set-up going on here, that they, to use a colloquial, they were smelling a rat. That we were setting it up by calling Ridgway at the last moment and then when the Defence objects to it saying we don't have enough time, and then we withdraw him and we attempt to call an expert in rebuttal. Nothing could be further from the truth. We've made it clear all the way along. We want to all General Ridgway because he has some familiarity with the case. But because of his position, he has limited availability. So we wish to confine the scope of his testimony to those particular areas and we would hope the Defence would limit its cross-examination to those issues upon which he would give his expert testimony. There's simply no set-up here. We don't plan to try and call an expert in rebuttal. We would have exactly the same problems we would have with General Ridgway, that is trying to get all the material to a new expert and to get them on top of it. We can't do that in this case. That's why we're after a more abstract or specific opinion on the two areas of law which we say will assist the Tribunal. My learned colleague, Mr. Morrissey, also alluded us to the fact or also said that he thought the general would be giving evidence on the ultimate issue. If he looks at the proposed deletions from the report, he'll see that anything that anything which seems to touch on the ultimate issue is gone from there and I make it clear we don't intend to ask the general issues on the ultimate issue, so they can rest assured on that. We don't intend to ask the general issues on the guilt or innocence of the accused but only as to the measures a commander should take in these circumstances, assuming notice of the crimes. Most of the matters which my learned colleague has raised are really matters of cross-examination, which can be dealt with in cross-examination. If they say the facts have changed, they are entitled to examine the expert on that. If Your Honours agree with the Defence, then it's a matter of weight, how much weight to give the expert opinion and the Prosecution has to live with that at the end of the day. Most of these are evidentiary matters which in our opinion can be well dealt with by the Defence in their cross-examination of the general, which we anticipate will be skilful. Those are the only matters I would raise at the moment, unless there's anything you wish us to respond to specifically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, since the Defence is going to file a motion this afternoon, so we are not going to discuss this matter any further in this sitting. But I have to remind the Defence that we have already had a motion of 28 pages at our hands. So I hope that the Defence motion should be very concise so that the Prosecution as well as the Bench could make a swift decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, Your Honour now know that there was a battalion of mice resubordinated to Mr. Halilovic in this operation. We will have those mice to nibble at our submission and eat it away and we will have that submission reduced in size greatly by the end of today and we'll have it in an acceptable form. But what we do need -- what we do need is for there to be some certainty about the OTP's response time because the time is ticking away now. And not just a matter of responding to the motion, but I think it's likely that the OTP would need at least some time to respond and of course they should be entitled to realistic time. But, Your Honours, there's a number of options open to the Tribunal in dealing with what we say. You might deal with this entirely and prevent them or you might impose some other outcome on them. But at the very least and without further -- without any further, the Prosecution should really provide a proper report. I just had it in front of me a moment ago Rule 94 about this. But could I just remind the Tribunal at the end of the day Rule 94 says that: "The full statement of any expert witness to be called by a party shall be disclosed within the time limit prescribed by the Chamber or the Pre-Trial Judge." And what we don't have now is that full statement. Now, we do not insist -- there's a type -- a period of 30 days is then mentioned concerning the response to that, that within 30 days of disclosure of that there has to be response by the Defence. We just need the Prosecutors to indicate -- to indicate whether they are prepared to do that, because if -- well, now, look -- I think, Your Honours, as I talk, I realise I'm probably trespassing into the area of the submission. What I'm anxious about is that we go through the process of our motion and the Prosecution's response and Your Honours' rule, there's very little time left after that. And the Prosecution, if they continue to refuse to give us a report, well it's going to create time delays and difficult -- well, it shouldn't do so, but that's what's going to happen obviously. So what I would ask is that the Prosecutors, if they do wish to persist with calling this witness, be ordered -- be ordered now to provide a full report or to indicate that they refuse to do so, so that that issue is finished with and cut and dry today. That is something that can be decided today, whether they are going to do that or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Re, are you ready to furnish the report to the other party and the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: We have furnished the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: How about the redacted one?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: We have. We provided it to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The Chamber has it, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I understand the redacted one has not been signed by the expert himself. It's done by the Prosecution and I wonder whether the procedure is over or not. I mean, you have to show that redacted report to the author himself and ask him to sign that redacted one which makes it more authentic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Well, of course we understand that, but our submission is that the purpose of the rule is to provide notice to the Defence. We've given notice to the Defence and in our submission at the moment the signature isn't going to change the nature of the notice. The notice is of the effect of the testimony, what the expert, we anticipate, will say. We can give a -- in any situation you can give a report to the other side with a signature on it. You come to the report and the expert rejects to three-quarters of the report and it goes. Or the the expert can come into the court and gives additional evidence as normally happens. Experts normally come into the court and give additional oral evidence on matters in their report. That's not unusual at all. And there's no additional report on the oral matters. So but the Defence is still on notice because they received the report. So I'm saying the policy purpose is to give notice, they have the notice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: So you mean that the Defence have already received the full report as well as the redacted report?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes, the redaction is the highlighted parts which we would propose to redact. The general hasn't signed it, but it's the same effect in terms of giving them notice of the parts we don't rely on in the report. So they know what we're not relying upon. That's good for them. We've taken out huge slabs of it in relation to Uzdol. They don't need to worry about that. That must limit the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Another matter is that an expert is called to testify as to the special areas beyond the other people's knowledge. And at this time, we need the CV of this expert so as to establish his expertise. As you said, he has some experience in Kosovo and the former Yugoslavia. I believe that's a very important matter. Of course an expert is called to give some opinion evidence on that because expert is entitled to do that. However, he should not touch upon those ultimate issues, especially the specific facts, because the witness is not a factual witness. He just gives some special -- some knowledge in the special areas. And in this way, I have to remind you that there are other practices in this Tribunal, that is we use expert report in the proceedings and the Prosecution just spend maybe 20 minutes to lead certain evidence to draw the Bench's attention to certain areas, then leaves most of the time for the cross-examination because eventually the expert report will be admitted into the evidence. This is another approach for us to do so. But anyway, I hope you could furnish the CV of that expert to the other party and to the Bench, if possible, today. And I hope we could get your response on Tuesday, next Tuesday, since we have a long weekend. And this Bench will make the best effort to make a decision as early as possible. By the way, are there any possibilities for us to hear this expert witness for a longer time? For instance, how about the weekend? If we could not finish him in one day, is it possible for us to sit on Saturday and Sunday?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: From the Prosecution's perspective it is. I have to make that inquiry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yeah, of course, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: We can certainly do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: It's just a suggestion on that, just to see the possibilities without prejudice to the final rulings of that oral decision on that issue, since we haven't received that motion yet. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Just on the CV, the first two paragraphs of the report actually details the lieutenant general's experience. Is that good enough for the Chamber and the Defence's requirements to assess the expertise of the general? He graduated in 1970; has a master of philosophy in international relations; did a specialist thesis on the impact of changes on the Soviet military doctrine and the correlation of forces in the region; commanded a tank regiment; commanded the 7th armoured brigade in Germany; commanded the UN Bosnia-Herzegovina command south-west sector in Gornji Vakuf, a sector which included Grabovica and Uzdol; senior staff positions in the Ministry of Defence, including colonel army programmes with the responsibility for the army's budgetary planning as director of operational capability and is director of general defence training and education. It's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: It's also mentioned that the present position of this expert witness, right?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It's not. It said he's "Chief of Staff in the NATO ARRC -- Rapid Reaction Corps; Chief of Staff in KFOR, Kosovo; overseas duty, Germany, Northern Ireland, Belize, Croatia, Bosnia, Kuwait, Macedonia and Kosovo; recently selected for promotion to lieutenant general and have taken up a new position." The new position he has is the chief of British military intelligence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I see. You might mention that in your proofing notes if the new CV is not required by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, the new CV, I don't require an updated CV. The Prosecutor has been good enough to indicate what's happened to him since that time. It's not the CV that we're worried by; it's what he's going to say in court. The challenge to expertise is not one that realities to someone's seniority or not but relates to whether they've got the expertise to say the opinion they're going to say. And as to the CV we don't take issue with that. We're not concerned by it. We're happy for the Prosecutor to provide anything additional by way of CV material if they want to, but we notice what's been said in court. Your Honour, it's the substance of what's going to be said that we're struggling with at the moment. We're in a bit of trouble. We are going to issue the motion this afternoon, but the motion is going to be that a report of David Re not be admitted. Because at the moment Andrew Ridgway hasn't signed the report that they want to rely on, nor do the Prosecution even tell you that he's even see it. So we're put in the position of shadow boxing here. We'll do it because of the time pressure, but it really is a very unsatisfactory situation for us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I quite understand that. I have nothing to say at this stage on this matter. Are there any other issues the parties would like to bring to the attention of this Bench?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Pardon me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: There are a number of outstanding matters that need to be dealt with. Would Your Honour excuse me, I have something to clarify with my learned colleague before I go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, some time ago the Prosecutors indicated to the Defence that they would assist with providing us with certain term relating to outstanding charges against the witnesses Alispahic and Delalic and the recently put-to-rest witness, Mujezinovic. Since that time some material has been apparently made available, but the Defence needs a letter from the Prosecutor to have permission to look at this material in Sarajevo. I'm advised that Mr. Weiner has indicated that he's perfectly happy to give us such a letter. So we don't ask for any intervention by the Chamber on that. Concerning the status of Mr. Delalic, we just want to know what the position is about his status insofar as the current court proceedings are concerned. That witness is coming next Tuesday and we wish to know what the status of him is. We think he's on trial for murder at the moment and there was some doubt about that. I'm not sure what's been put on his Visa and how that's all been handled. We want to know what his status is from the Prosecutors, so we're awaiting a response to that and perhaps they would be in a position to respond to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: We, I made a check a few days ago, Your Honour, and the information we received is there is an outstanding charge of murder from the famous wedding murder that occurred I think in 1991. He is supposedly on bail, on a very high bail which he has put his house up as a surety or one or two homes as a surety. We have not been able to confirm, and since he is arriving today, we will be able to confirm with him and his attorney and notify counsel. But we were told -- as counsel knows, we provided them with the indictment. He has been charged with that murder and he is currently on a bail situation. We will be able to confirm that matter today with his counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I'm grateful for that and I'm satisfied with that response, Your Honour. The next issue is the proofing notes regarding Mr. Delalic. Your Honours, we just want to be sure that we have those proofing notes in a timely fashion. We can't have those at a late time. Your Honours, we got the proofing notes with the last witness very late, but that was by agreement because the Prosecutors were under pressure, and he's a professional witness. I agreed with Mr. Weiner that that should be done at a late stage and I should say I called Mr. Weiner very late at night and he was working on it we spoke about it. We consented to it being done at a late stage there and so it was legitimate. But no such thing can be done with Mr. Delalic. We need those proofing notes at the very latest by 9.00 a.m. on Monday so we can have a full day to consider what's in those proofing notes. That would leave the Prosecutor with today and Saturday and Sunday to deal with him, which, two days would be -- we hope would be sufficient for the Prosecutor's purposes. But in any event we say we need that to be done by 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. How soon could you provide those proofing notes?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I want to say to expedite the proofing situation we sent all the proofing notes to Mr. Delalic all his previous statements by mail to Sarajevo, so when he would came here he would be able to start immediately as opposed to when the witness arrives he starts to review all of his previous statements. Everything was sent so we're able to start immediately today and move the proofing much quicker. So hopefully able to get the proofing notes out Monday, but I will speak with Attorney Chana.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I hope you could furnish the proofing notes as required by the Defence, that is before 9.00, Monday morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I will relay the witness to Attorney Chana. I'm not doing the proofing, Your Honour. I will tell Attorney Chana the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, you should do your best.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: We will do our best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any other matters?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, concerning Mr. Delalic there's another matter. In respect of Mr. Delalic it's apparent from the statements made by Delalic -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Ms. Chana just sent a letter -- an e-mail note that she could provide them by 1.00 p.m. on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we are sitting in the morning, that is 9.00, on the 17th of May. So I believe that at least Defence needs 24 hours to study it and to deal with it. Of course it all depends on how extensive those proofing notes are and usually the proofing notes only should touch upon the matters which is something new from the previous statement rather than go over all the testimonies of the witness. So, Mr. Weiner, I hope you could give some advice to Ms. Chana and ask her to do her best to furnish the proofing notes before 9.00 Monday morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'll notify her and I know she'll do her best. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, as to Mr. Delalic, it's apparent from Mr. Delalic's own previous statements that he had numerous discussions and meetings with an OTP investigator -- with OTP investigators and in particular Nikolai Mikhailov. So what we want to be provided with is all notes and records relating to those meetings, whether or not a formal statement was taken on those occasions. Now, those notes and records must be in the possession of the OTP. It's an important matter. It occurred -- particularly the year 1998 that we can assist the Prosecutor with our areas of interest. We're particularly interested in 1998, but of course all subsequent meetings must also be covered if there are any subsequent meetings. But it's evident in late 1997 and early 1998 there were a number of such meetings between Ramiz Delalic and Nikolai Mikhailov. Now, Mikhailov must have taken such notes and such notes must be in the possession of the Prosecutor, so we ask that they be provided to us for the purposes of dealing with this witness when he comes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We've looked in the past. There are numerous statements from this witness that have been -- that were taken and were provided. If there are any notes, we have no problem to turn them over unless there was something of a nature of work product. But whatever we've had we've turned over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. I hope you could do a research during this weekend to see whether there are any records or transcripts for those interviews.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'll have the investigator, Mr. Brun, take a look today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: As I said, we have looked in the past.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's the final matter I -- just as a matter of caution, I think we should go into the private session for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We'll go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Are there any other issues that the parties would like to mention at this stage?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, there was one that I missed and this is the last of the issues I have raised. There have in the past been discussions that the Prosecutor would provide an updated list of victims, of persons who the Prosecution might say were murdered. Now, it's quite evident that things have changed in that regard since the start of the case, so it might be that the Prosecutor -- they're not go engage in debate with us about it, it's a question of who they now assert have been murdered, who they're persisting with in that regard. And it would be of assistance if that was done. So we ask whether the Prosecutor are prepared to comply with that and indicate whether they have a list of those or whether they could by early next week provide a list of those who they say can be found beyond a reasonable doubt to have been murdered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, I believe this Bench asked for this list during a 65 ter meeting. And the Prosecution at that time promised us to furnish us with such kind of list.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I was under the view that that was a submission for the 98 bis hearing or at the end of the case. If it's a submission as we've done in a previous case, in the Strugar case, that submission was made at the 98 bis as to what the evidence was at the end of the Prosecution as to each building that had been damaged, out of the 400-plus buildings that were charged exactly which buildings were damaged. In this case we thought in our 98 bis submission to file something on a sheet of paper or just go through person by person and what the evidence is as to each of those individuals. But if the Court wants it ahead of time, we can provide it ahead of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Of course the most appropriate time is for the 98 bis submissions, which is a kind of response from the request of the Defence concerning of the acquittal issues. But however, if you are in the position to do that in an earlier time, I believe that it will be welcomed by the Bench as well as by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: All right, Your Honour. That will be fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: So you'll file that list in a week's time?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I don't know if I can do it in a week's time because now we have to respond to two, probably three motions next week because of the motion will be filed today, the motion that was filed a few days ago, and I think there was another one that was filed. But probably the week after we could get that in, which would still be a week prior -- a few weeks prior to the 98 bis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. I understand that you have a very busy weekend since some of the responses will be filed on Monday, 9.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Although -- although -- Monday is still a holiday.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: As you said, make your best effort to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I believe that's all for this hearing and we'll resume at next Tuesday at 9.00 in the morning in the same courtroom. And I wish everybody a good weekend. The hearing for today is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 17th day of May, 2005, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 10.35 a.m.,
